extracted.intended_audience: writers who give or receive feedback in workshops or with writing buddies
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for giving and receiving peer feedback on short fiction (or similar creative writing) in workshops or informal critique groups. Focuses on reading strategy, quantity and tone of comments, interpreting feedback, and author mindset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the work at least twice
rubrics_metrics.description: Before giving feedback, read the work at least twice. The first time through, just read. Don’t even hold your pen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you can, take a break after the first read, then come back with your pen and set to work. The first read is for experiencing the piece; subsequent reads are for analysis and notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: First read without marking; annotate on second pass
rubrics_metrics.description: On your initial read-through, avoid making marks; return later to annotate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This repeats and clarifies the 'read twice' advice: the unmarked first read helps you see the work whole and avoid premature judgments; the later pass lets you produce useful, focused commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for four comments/notes per page
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a roughly consistent quantity of feedback: the author recommends about four comments or notes per page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer likes to put check marks next to things that work; sometimes that's all you have on a page. Try to balance quantity with usefulness — regular, specific notes help the author revise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give positive feedback (mark what works) as well as criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell authors what works for you; positive marks are as valuable as criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use check marks next to elements that succeed; hearing about what works is just as important as hearing about what doesn't, and positive notes can be sparse but meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t push your own expectations onto the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid imposing your personal expectations or assumptions about how the story 'should' be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pretend you're reading the New Yorker — if you don't understand something, consider it might be you. The author may be shifting POVs or time on purpose to reflect character state of mind. Don't be too quick to judge; interpret generously and consider authorial intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat conflicting feedback as a diagnostic sign
rubrics_metrics.description: If readers give conflicting responses, interpret that as an indication 'something isn't landing on the page.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the analogy offered: conflicting feedback is like a fever — a symptom of a deeper infection. The author must diagnose what's causing the split reactions and address that underlying issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't be discouraged by unresolved elements; reader confusion can be useful
rubrics_metrics.description: If aspects like theme or certain plot details aren't yet resolved, this isn't necessarily bad; initial author uncertainty can preserve surprise and discovery for readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your confusion may become the reader's delight because the story won't feel telegraphed. As you, the author, discovers answers during revision, readers will discover them too and the story can be stronger for that gradual revelation.
